drills.q: Why does adding two bits need two output bits?
options: Two ones sum to two, which does not fit in one bit
One output is the result and the other is an error flag
To allow signed as well as unsigned addition
Because the inputs are two bits
drills.why: The low bit of the sum and a carry into the next position. That is the whole reason a half adder has two outputs rather than one.

drills.q: In a half adder, the sum output is which function?
options: Exclusive or
And
Or
Nand
drills.why: The sum is 1 exactly when the inputs differ. The carry is 1 exactly when both are 1, which is and. Both are parts already built, so a half adder needs no new idea.

drills.q: Why is it called a half adder?
options: It cannot accept a carry coming in, and every position except the lowest
It handles only half the bits of an operand
It produces half the outputs of a full adder
It is half the size of a full adder
drills.why: A full adder takes three inputs, and a wide adder is full adders chained with each carry out feeding the next carry in.

drills.q: A full adder is built from:
options: Two half adders and an or
Two half adders and an and
Three half adders
A half adder and a multiplexer
drills.why: Add the operands, then add the carry to that sum. Both additions can produce a carry and both cannot at once, so an or gathers them.

options: Each position waiting for the carry from the position below it
Carries arriving from several positions at once
A carry that wraps from the top back to the bottom
Noise on the carry line
drills.why: So the time to add is one adder's delay times the number of bits, and at any real width that is the longest path in the machine.

options: Computing per position whether a carry is generated or passed along, then
Using faster transistors on the carry path
Adding the low and high halves in parallel and correcting afterwards
Running the carry chain at a higher clock
drills.why: That gives delay proportional to the logarithm of the width rather than to the width. It costs gates, which is why it is a Part III subject.

drills.q: To subtract in two's complement you:
options: Invert one operand and set the carry in
Use a row of full subtractors with borrow
Negate the result of an addition
Compare first, then subtract the smaller from the larger
drills.why: a - b is a + (not b) + 1. Inverting is one gate per bit, and adding one is free because the adder already has a carry input nothing was using.

drills.q: What makes one control bit enough for both add and subtract?
options: It feeds an exclusive or on each bit of one operand and also the carry in
It selects between two separate circuits
It switches the adder into a different mode
It inverts the result afterwards
drills.why: An exclusive or with the control passes the operand through when the control is 0 and inverts it when it is 1. The same bit supplies the plus one.

drills.q: Where does the saving in subtraction actually come from?
options: The choice to represent negative numbers in two's complement
A clever arrangement of gates
The carry input being unused
Reusing the adder rather than building a subtractor
drills.why: It is the first time in this handbook that a representation choice buys hardware. Sign and magnitude needs a comparison, a subtraction and a decision about the sign: three circuits where you wanted one.

drills.q: Why is sign-and-magnitude a worse representation for hardware?
options: Adding a positive and a negative number needs comparison and a sign
It cannot represent zero
It wastes a bit
It is harder for people to read
drills.why: Two's complement gives the top bit a negative weight instead of a flag meaning, and then one adder handles signed and unsigned operands unchanged.

drills.q: How does a machine test whether two values are equal?
options: Subtract them and check whether the result is zero
Compare them bit by bit in a comparator
Look them up in a table
Exclusive-or them and count the ones
drills.why: Which is an or across the result bits, inverted. A machine does not need comparison hardware: it needs an adder and somewhere to look at what came out.

drills.q: How does it test whether one value is less than another?
options: Subtract and look at the sign, or equivalently at the borrow
Compare the high bits and then the low bits
Count the set bits in each
Repeatedly subtract one until one reaches zero
drills.why: The flags a branch looks at are the leftovers of an arithmetic operation that already happened, which is what the unit on control is built on.

drills.q: An increment costs nothing extra because:
options: The adder already has a carry input on its lowest position
Adding one is a special case the hardware detects
Incrementing is a shift
It uses the same gates as a decrement
drills.why: And the counter in unit 010 is that increment with a register round it, which is also why a jump turns out to be a parallel load rather than special machinery.

drills.q: Why is a real arithmetic unit built as an adder with control bits in front?
options: Each control bit changes what the operands look like on the way in, so
Because separate circuits would not fit
Because control bits are faster than gates
To allow the operations to run in parallel
drills.why: nand2tetris reaches eighteen useful functions from one adder with six control bits that zero, invert and select the inputs and the output.

drills.q: Why is a negate-output control bit nearly free?
options: It is one exclusive or per bit, where building both polarities and
Inversion is free in CMOS
It reuses the subtract control
The output is already available inverted
drills.why: It is the same argument as unit 002, one layer up: inverting is cheap and having both polarities available is not.
